claim: Two-photon phosphorescence lifetime microscopy (2PLM) has been used to measure oxygen partial pressure (Po2) in the rodent brain.
source: The synthesis of new two-photon phosphorescent oxygen sensors such as PtP-C343 and the use of two-photon phosphorescence lifetime microscopy (2PLM) have revolutionized measurements of oxygen partial pressure (Po2) in the rodent brain (Finikova et al., 2007; Finikova et al., 2008; Wilson et al., 2011; Esipova et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work establishing this technique

claim: 2PLM has allowed mapping of Po2 in vessels and neuropil of the neocortex to a depth of several hundred micrometers.
source: This approach has allowed mapping of Po2 in vessels and neuropil of the neocortex (Sakadzić et al., 2010; Devor et al., 2011; Lecoq et al., 2011; Yaseen et al., 2011; Sakadžić et al., 2014; Lyons et al., 2016; Sakadžić et al., 2016; Kisler et al., 2018; Moeini et al., 2018) and olfactory bulb (Lecoq et al., 2011; Parpaleix et al., 2013; Lyons et al., 2016), to a depth of several hundred micrometers.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations documenting this capability

claim: 2PLM's micrometer spatial resolution revealed the presence of erythrocyte-associated transients (EATs), Po2 transients associated with individual erythrocytes.
source: 2PLM's micrometer spatial resolution and the possibility to monitor simultaneously Po2 and individual red blood cells (RBCs) in capillaries revealed the presence of erythrocyte-associated transients (EATs), Po2 transients that are associated with individual erythrocytes (Lecoq et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: In anesthetized mice, Po2 between two EAT peaks is at near-equilibrium with Po2 in the neuropil surrounding capillaries.
source: We reported that in anesthetized mice, Po2 between two EAT peaks is at near-equilibrium with Po2 in the neuropil surrounding capillaries, providing a unique and noninvasive way to measure brain oxygenation (Parpaleix et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work by the authors

claim: Resting Po2 values in awake mice are about ~25 mmHg in olfactory bulb glomeruli and in the superficial layers of the somatosensory cortex (layers I to IV).
source: Using this approach in awake mice chronically implanted with a glass window and trained for several weeks in order to minimize stress, we then reported resting Po2 values of about ~25 mmHg in olfactory bulb glomeruli and in the superficial layers of the somatosensory cortex, that is from layer I to IV (Lyons et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work by the authors

claim: Chronic window preparation imposes removing the scalp and cranial bone, which play an important role as thermal insulators and temperature regulators.
source: However, our chronic window preparation imposed removing the scalp and the cranial bone, which play an important role as thermal insulators and temperature regulators.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about the thermal properties of scalp and bone

claim: Imaging through a glass window lowers brain temperature in acute mice preparations, causing depolarization of neurons and changes of cortical network properties.
source: The thermal consequences of imaging through a glass window have been previously investigated in acute mice preparations, revealing a depolarization of neurons and changes of cortical network properties (Kalmbach and Waters, 2012; Podgorski and Ranganathan, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: Resting brain surface temperature recovers to about 37°C within few days post-surgery in mice chronically implanted with a glass window.
source: Here, we investigated the relationship between temperature and blood flow parameters or oxygenation in small capillaries of the mouse olfactory bulb, anesthetized and awake. We show that i) resting brain surface temperature recovers to about 37°C within few days post-surgery
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Heat is constantly lost through the glass window chronically implanted over the olfactory bulb.
source: We show that i) resting brain surface temperature recovers to about 37°C within few days post-surgery and, ii) heat is constantly lost through the glass window chronically implanted over the olfactory bulb.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: 2PLM with a cool water immersion objective at room temperature decreases brain temperature by ~2–3°C.
source: 2PLM and standard two-photon imaging with a cool (room temperature) water immersion objective decreases brain temperature by ~2–3°C
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Imaging with a cool water immersion objective causes a significant drop of resting capillary blood flow and red blood cell (RBC) velocity.
source: 2PLM and standard two-photon imaging with a cool (room temperature) water immersion objective decreases brain temperature by ~2–3°C, causing a significant drop of resting capillary blood flow and red blood cell (RBC) velocity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Imaging with a cool water immersion objective lowers all Po2 parameters, measured after taking into account the temperature-dependence of the oxygen sensor PtP-C343.
source: It also lowers all Po2 parameters, measured after taking into account the temperature-dependence of the oxygen sensor PtP-C343.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Heating the objective to correct brain temperature or imaging with a dry objective are required to determine the true physiological values of capillary blood flow and brain oxygenation.
source: Heating the objective to correct brain temperature or imaging with a dry objective are required to determine the true physiological values of capillary blood flow and brain oxygenation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing different imaging conditions

claim: Surgery associated with general anesthesia caused a temperature decrease at the brain surface that outlasted anesthesia and 2–4 days were necessary for brain temperature recovery to ~37°C.
source: Surgery associated with general anesthesia caused a temperature decrease at the brain surface that outlasted anesthesia and 2–4 days were necessary for brain temperature recovery to ~37°C (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b

claim: In awake animals, temperature immediately above the glass window was about ~35–36°C, indicating that the brain constantly loses heat to the room environment.
source: In awake animals, temperature immediately above the glass window was about ~35–36°C, indicating that the brain constantly loses heat to the room environment (maintained at 21–23°C).
evidence: Supported by experimental temperature measurements

claim: Adding water between the window and the objective caused a transient drop of the surface brain temperature by 5–10°C that partially recovered within few minutes.
source: Adding water between the window and the objective, caused a transient drop of the surface brain temperature by 5–10°C that partially recovered within few minutes.
evidence: Supported by experimental temperature measurements

claim: In awake mice, brain temperature stabilized at ~2°C below the resting value (without immersion) and temperature recovered to its resting value upon heating the objective.
source: In awake mice, it stabilized at ~2°C below the resting value (without immersion) and temperature recovered to its resting value upon heating the objective (Figure 1b,c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1b and 1c

claim: Body core temperature was constantly maintained at ~37°C throughout the whole experiment.
source: Note that all measurements were done while the body core temperature was constantly maintained at ~37°C throughout the whole experiment.
evidence: Describes experimental control condition

claim: Phosphorescence lifetime of PtP-C343 is temperature-dependent.
source: As phosphorescence lifetime of PtP-C343 is temperature-dependent (Finikova et al., 2008), we first established PtP-C343 calibration curves at the mean temperatures observed in our various imaging conditions, prior to any in vivo imaging experiment.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: Calibration curves were shifted to the right when lowering temperature.
source: Note that calibration curves were shifted to the right when lowering temperature (Figure 2b), the insets indicating the necessity of using the adequate curve to convert the decay tau to Po2.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b

claim: In awake mice imaged with the air dry objective, resting RBC velocity per capillary was 0.75 +/- 0.09 mm/s.
source: In awake mice imaged with the air dry objective, resting RBC velocity per capillary was 0.75 + /- 0.09 mm/s
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: In awake mice imaged with the air dry objective, resting RBC flow was 44 +/- 5 RBC/s.
source: In awake mice imaged with the air dry objective, resting RBC velocity per capillary was 0.75 + /- 0.09 mm/s, resting RBC flow 44 + /- 5 RBC/s
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: In awake mice imaged with the air dry objective, resting Po2 Mean was 42 +/- 3 mmHg.
source: In awake mice imaged with the air dry objective, resting RBC velocity per capillary was 0.75 + /- 0.09 mm/s, resting RBC flow 44 + /- 5 RBC/s and resting Po2 Mean 42 + /- 3 mmHg.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: Imaging the same capillaries through the water immersion objective at room temperature decreased RBC velocity, RBC flow, and Po2 Mean by ~33%, 22% and 20%, respectively.
source: Imaging the same capillaries through the water immersion objective at room temperature decreased the three vascular parameters by ~33%, 22% and 20%, respectively (RBC velocity was 0.5 + /- 0.1 mm/s, RBC flow 35 + /- 5 RBC/s, Po2 Mean 34 + /- 3 mmHg)
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements comparing conditions

claim: Resting capillary hemodynamics and Po2 Mean recovered to their resting values upon restoring brain temperature to ~37°C by heating the objective.
source: Interestingly, resting capillary hemodynamics and Po2 Mean recovered to their resting values upon restoring brain temperature to ~37°C (i.e. heating the objective and correcting for the working distance change, see Materials and methods) (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a

claim: Po2 at the RBC border (Po2 RBC) and at mid distance between two RBCs (Po2 interRBC) decreased by ~14% and ~26% during imaging with a cool objective.
source: Analysis of EATs using our previous approach (Lyons et al., 2016; Parpaleix et al., 2013), revealed that Po2 at the RBC border (Po2 RBC) and at mid distance between two RBCs (Po2 interRBC) (see Figure 3b inset) decreased by ~14% and~26% during imaging with a cool objective, an effect reversible upon heating the objective.
evidence: Supported by experimental data with reference to Figure 3b

claim: Po2 interRBC reports Po2 in the nearby neuropil.
source: As Po2 interRBC reports Po2 in the nearby neuropil (Parpaleix et al., 2013), these data demonstrate that resting tissue Po2 in glomeruli is about 31.4 mmHg
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: Resting tissue Po2 in glomeruli is about 31.4 mmHg.
source: As Po2 interRBC reports Po2 in the nearby neuropil (Parpaleix et al., 2013), these data demonstrate that resting tissue Po2 in glomeruli is about 31.4 mmHg (Figure 3b, middle).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b

claim: In olfactory bulb capillaries, resting hemoglobin saturation is about 70% and principally exists as oxyhemoglobin.
source: Given that Po2 RBC is representative of the Po2 level inside RBCs and using previous values of the Hill coefficient and P50 for mouse hemoglobin (Uchida et al., 1998), resting Po2 RBC values suggest that in olfactory bulb capillaries, resting hemoglobin saturation is about 70% and principally exists as oxyhemoglobin (Figure 3b, right).
evidence: Inferred from Po2 RBC measurements using established hemoglobin properties from cited work

claim: Heating the objective significantly increased RBC velocity, RBC flow and Po2 in glomerular capillaries in anesthetized mice.
source: We thus tested the reproducibility of our findings in mice implanted with a chronic glass window, anesthetized with a mixture of ketamine-medetomidine (100 mg kg−1 and 0.4 mg kg−one body mass, respectively) and supplemented with oxygen (reaching 30% in the inhaled air). Heating the objective had similar consequences: it significantly increased RBC velocity, RBC flow and Po2 in glomerular capillaries (Figure 3c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c

claim: With 30% oxygen inhaled, resting Po2 Mean with the objective at room temperature (65 +/- 8 mm Hg) was much higher than that in awake mice breathing normal air (34 +/- 3 mm Hg).
source: Note that with 30% oxygen inhaled (instead of 21%), resting Po2 Mean with the objective at room temperature (65 + /- 8 mm Hg) was much higher than that in awake mice breathing normal air (34 + /- 3 mm Hg).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements comparing conditions

claim: Thinned-skull cortical windows have been used for decades to image blood flow dynamics with laser Doppler flowmetry or laser speckle.
source: Thinned-skull cortical windows have been used for decades to image blood flow dynamics with laser Doppler flowmetry (Gerrits et al., 1998) or laser speckle (Zakharov et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Polished and reinforced thinned skull (PoRTS) allows long term imaging of neurons and glial cells with improved imaging quality, stability and without inflammation.
source: It has also become a very popular technique for imaging functional hyperemia using TPLSM, with the additional reinforcement of a glass cover slip (Polished and reinforced thinned skull (PoRTS)), which allows long term imaging of neurons and glial cells with improved imaging quality, stability and without inflammation (Drew et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: 3–4 days were required for the brain to recover a stable brain temperature (37.7 +/- 0.2°C) in mice with a glass reinforced thinned skull over the barrel cortex.
source: As with the glass window preparation, 3–4 days were required for the brain to recover a stable brain temperature (37.7 + /- 0.2°C) (Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b

claim: Imaging with the water immersion objective at room temperature lowered the surface temperature by ~3°C (34.5 +/- 0.4°C) in mice with reinforced thinned-skull preparation.
source: Imaging with the water immersion objective at room temperature lowered the surface temperature by ~3°C (34.5 + /- 0.4°C), an effect reversible upon heating the objective (36.9 + /- 0.4°C, n = 3 mice).
evidence: Supported by experimental temperature measurements

claim: Resting RBC velocity, RBC flow and mean Po2 increased by 18.4%, 27.5% and 33%, respectively, upon temperature restoration in mice with reinforced thinned-skull preparation.
source: Similarly, resting RBC velocity, RBC flow and mean Po2 increased by 18.4%, 27.5% and 33%, respectively, upon temperature restauration (Figure 4c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c

claim: When imaging with the reinforced thinned-skull preparation, the thin bone layer does not protect against the thermal effect caused by the objective and immersion liquid.
source: We conclude that when imaging with the reinforced thinned-skull preparation, the thin bone layer does not protect against the thermal effect caused by the objective and immersion liquid.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing similar thermal effects as with glass window

claim: The thermal effects of light during photoactivation and two-photon imaging are widely recognized.
source: The thermal effects of light during photoactivation (Stujenske et al., 2015; Arias-Gil et al., 2016; Shin et al., 2016; Picot et al., 2018) and two-photon imaging (Podgorski and Ranganathan, 2016) are widely recognized and there is a general consensus that light intensity should be kept as low as possible.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work

claim: As opposed to what occurs in the acute preparation, brain temperature recovers to 37°C after a few days in chronic window preparation.
source: We find that as opposed to what occurs in the acute preparation, brain temperature recovers to 37°C after a few days, suggesting that, i) there is an adaptation of local blood flow, ii) the brain constantly loses heat to the air above the glass, as supported by the temperature gradient across the two sides of the glass window.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and inferred mechanisms

claim: There is an adaptation of local blood flow following chronic window implantation.
source: We find that as opposed to what occurs in the acute preparation, brain temperature recovers to 37°C after a few days, suggesting that, i) there is an adaptation of local blood flow
evidence: Inferred from temperature recovery data

claim: The drop in oxygenation principally results from the decrease of blood flow, rather than from minor changes of the affinity of hemoglobin to oxygen, the solubility and diffusion of oxygen.
source: We believe that this drop in oxygenation principally results from the decrease of blood flow, rather than from minor changes of the affinity of hemoglobin to oxygen (Dash and Bassingthwaighte, 2010), the solubility (Christmas and Bassingthwaighte, 2017) and diffusion of oxygen.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations with supporting citations

claim: The true physiological capillary Po2 Mean in glomeruli is about 42 mm Hg.
source: These findings reveal that our previous data acquired in the awake animal and in the same imaging conditions (Lyons et al., 2016) (with a water immersion objective at room temperature) have to be corrected and Po2 values increased. We now suggest that in glomeruli, the true physiological capillary Po2 Mean is about 42 mm Hg
evidence: Supported by experimental data correcting previous measurements

claim: The true physiological Po2 Inter RBC (Po2 in the neuropil) in glomeruli is about 31 mmHg.
source: We now suggest that in glomeruli, the true physiological capillary Po2 Mean is about 42 mm Hg and Po2 Inter RBC, that is Po2 in the neuropil, about 31 mmHg.
evidence: Supported by experimental data correcting previous measurements

claim: Resting capillary blood flow and RBC velocity should be increased by 22% and 33%, respectively, when considering imaging with a dry objective as the real control condition.
source: Similarly resting capillary blood flow and RBC velocity should be increased by 22% and 33%, respectively, considering imaging with a dry objective as the real control condition.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing imaging conditions

claim: The quality of imaging with immersion objectives is superior and also require less laser power than with an air objective.
source: Furthermore, the quality of imaging with immersion objectives is superior and also require less laser power than with an air objective, an important consideration for avoiding heating, and potentially capillary stalls.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about optical properties of objectives

claim: Anesthesia lowered resting brain temperature and cerebral blood flow.
source: As expected (Zhu et al., 2009; Shirey et al., 2015; Suzuki et al., 2018), anesthesia lowered resting brain temperature and cerebral blood flow.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work and experimental observations

claim: Imaging with the objective at room temperature in anesthetized mice further decreased the temperature to 32.4°C.
source: Imaging with the objective at room temperature further decreased the temperature to 32.4°C.
evidence: Supported by experimental temperature measurements

claim: In all previous studies using TPLSM in anesthetized animals, resting vascular parameters (blood flow/velocity and Po2) below the glass window were not truly physiological even when global anesthesia was monitored carefully.
source: This indicates that in all previous studies using TPLSM in anesthetized animals, including ours, resting vascular parameters (blood flow/velocity and Po2) below the glass window were not truly physiological even when global anesthesia was monitored carefully.
evidence: Inferred from experimental findings about temperature effects

claim: The reinforced thinned-skull window does not ameliorate the thermal loss.
source: Finally, although the reinforced thinned-skull window is a less invasive preparation with significant advantages for TPLSM imaging, unfortunately it does not ameliorate the thermal loss.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing preparations

claim: Some phosphorescence can be generated at the level of the remaining bone in reinforced thinned-skull preparation.
source: In particular, as some phosphorescence can be generated at the level of the remaining bone, we do not advise the use of the reinforced thinned-skull for 2PLM measurements of Po2 in depth.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: TPLSM and 2PLM modify brain activity, oxygenation and blood supply, unless temperature is corrected to its physiological value.
source: To conclude, TPLSM and 2PLM modify brain activity, oxygenation and blood supply, unless temperature is corrected to its physiological value.
evidence: Supported by experimental data throughout the study

claim: Two-photon imaging was performed in small capillaries of the glomerular layer with diameter 3.1 +/- 0.5 µm.
source: Two-photon imaging was performed in small capillaries of the glomerular layer (diameter: 3.1+ /- 0.5, mean+/-std).
evidence: Describes experimental measurements

claim: Temperature changes due to two-photon scanning per se were detected by the brain surface thermocouple but were minute compared to changes caused by the water immersion objective.
source: Temperature changes due to two-photon scanning per se (Podgorski and Ranganathan, 2016; Picot et al., 2018) were detected by the brain surface thermocouple but not further considered, as they were minute in view of the changes causes by the water immersion objective.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations with citations to prior work

claim: All imaging experiments were performed after a minimum delay of 5 days post-surgery.
source: All imaging experiments were thus performed after a minimum delay of 5 days.
evidence: Describes experimental protocol

claim: The oxygen sensor penetrates the thin layer of bone left below the glass in reinforced thinned-skull preparation and generates a two-photon surface excitation when imaging the tissue in depth.
source: We had previously avoided the use of this approach for 2PLM measurements, as the oxygen sensor penetrates the thin layer of bone left below the glass and generates a two-photon surface excitation when imaging the tissue in depth.
evidence: Based on experimental observations

claim: Po2 measurements in mice with reinforced thinned-skull were limited to vessels from the upper part of layer 2/3, that is <180 µm from the surface.
source: During 2PLM experiments in mice with reinforced thinned-skull, we verified that in each case, some phosphorescence was generated in the thin bone layer. As a result, we limited our Po2 measurements to vessels from the upper part of layer 2/3, that is <180 µm from the surface.
evidence: Describes experimental protocol based on observed limitations
